summary:
Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in the Cayman Islands in 2001 by an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

In August 2009 members of the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the Cayman Islands' draft constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording citizens less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

Relationship status moved through the courts rather than the statute book. Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the prohibition on same-sex marriage in March 2019; the Court of Appeal reversed that ruling in August 2019, leaving the statutory ban in force, while the line of authority recognising overseas same-sex marriages for their immigration effects survived.

In December 2020 immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had wed in Ireland. The Court of Appeal held that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds.

Public visibility carries official backing. Around 600 people joined the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade on 7 August 2021, among them the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly. Participants were asked to refrain from excessive displays of affection, a condition organisers set in response to public-space sensitivities.
tangentialFactors:
The Cayman Islands stands under a United Kingdom framework in which London may legislate for the territory directly, the mechanism used to decriminalise same-sex intimacy in 2001 when the local legislature declined to act. The 2009 dispute over the draft constitution shows the same channel of pressure applied to the scope of anti-discrimination protection, with the parent parliament pressing for inclusion and the Foreign and Commonwealth Office defending the draft's open-ended list of discrimination grounds.

Judicial and legislative sequencing defines the territory's record on relationship recognition. The Grand Court acted first in March 2019, the Court of Appeal narrowed the outcome in August 2019, and the immigration authorities applied the surviving recognition principle in December 2020 without a corresponding amendment to the marriage statute.

Official participation in the August 2021 Pride parade, at which the premier and the governor marched alongside ministers and legislators, sits alongside organisers' own restraint condition on public affection. High-level attendance and that condition describe the same public-space environment rather than opposite readings of it.
localsOnly:
Same-sex couples cannot marry in the Cayman Islands: the statutory ban reinstated by the Court of Appeal in August 2019 remains in force. What residents retain is recognition of marriages performed elsewhere, applied so far through immigration decisions, with the Court of Appeal grounding that recognition in unequal treatment on sexual-orientation grounds.

The unequal age of consent left by the 2001 decriminalisation continues to govern consensual conduct among residents, since no legislative correction followed the Order in Council.

Organisers of the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation's first Pride parade asked participants to limit displays of affection in public space, a condition that applies to residents and visitors attending the event alike.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether hate-crime provisions cover sexual orientation or gender identity in the Cayman Islands, nor whether anti-discrimination law names gender identity among its grounds. The 2009 exchange indicates that the draft constitution's list of discrimination grounds was contested, but the sources do not record the final content of that list.

No sourced material addresses gender-marker or identity-document rules, access to facilities, healthcare or transition-related care, screening at the border, or next-of-kin and partner standing beyond the immigration decisions described here.

Whether United Kingdom legislation on legal recognition of gender extends to the Cayman Islands is not stated in these sources. Enforcement of the unequal age of consent, and any prosecutions under it, are likewise not sourced.
